label: Two-Variable Models
overview: SAT data questions ask you to interpret and use equations that model real-world relationships between two variables. These models can be linear (constant rate of change), quadratic (parabolic growth/decay), or exponential (percentage growth/decay). The key skill is reading the equation's parameters — slope, intercepts, and constants — in the context of the problem.

keyFormulas.name: Linear model
keyFormulas.latex: y = mx + b \quad (\text{constant rate of change})

keyFormulas.name: Quadratic model
keyFormulas.latex: y = ax^2 + bx + c \quad (\text{rate of change itself changes})

workedExamples.problem: The model P = 1200(1.03)^t gives the population of a town t years after 2010. What was the population in 2010, and what is the annual growth rate?

steps.title: Interpret the base
steps.content: The base 1.03 = 1 + 0.03 means the population grows by 3% per year.

commonMistakes.mistake: Misidentifying an exponential model as linear
commonMistakes.fix: Linear models add a constant amount each period; exponential models multiply by a constant ratio. Check whether the rate of change is constant (linear) or the ratio is constant (exponential).

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the y-intercept with the slope in a linear model
commonMistakes.fix: In y = mx + b: b is the starting value (x = 0), m is the rate of change per unit of x.

quickTip: Read the question carefully: it usually asks what the coefficient or exponent base represents in context, not just a numerical answer. Connect each parameter to its real-world meaning.
